headline: Hollywood Finally Discovers Tech Villains, Only 15 Years Late
subheadline: Four fall films expose billionaire malfeasance that venture capitalists funded with eyes wide open.
body_html:
Hollywood is experiencing a sudden moral awakening. Four films hitting theaters this fall have trained their cameras on Silicon Valley's most powerful and controversial figures: Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman, and Elizabeth Holmes. Each represents a different flavor of tech billionaire pathology—the erratic visionary, the privacy-indifferent monopolist, the narrative fabricator, and the outright fraudster, respectively. Apparently, the entertainment industry has just now decided these men make compelling antagonists, despite their decades-long careers of providing actual, well-documented material for screenplays.

What makes this moment delicious is the temporal gap between Hollywood's discovery and venture capital's funding decisions. These four figures didn't emerge from nowhere in 2024. Musk has been running Twitter into the ground for over a year; Zuckerberg has been testifying before Congress about Facebook's harms since 2018; Altman has been steering OpenAI through a governance crisis that would make most board members weep; Holmes was literally convicted of fraud in 2022. The VCs who funded their companies, cheered their Series rounds, and collected their eventual returns had ringside seats to the dysfunction. Yet capital flowed anyway, because narrative lag is a feature of the venture ecosystem, not a bug.

The VC industry operates on a systematic delay between evidence and consequence. When a founder displays the kind of megalomania, operational recklessness, or ethical flexibility that later becomes fodder for prestige dramas, early-stage investors interpret these traits as "founder-market fit" or "visionary tenacity." By the time Hollywood catches up—by the time the press, the general public, and eventually the filmmakers decide a figure is worth scrutinizing—the venture players have already exited. They've already collected their multiples. The moral accounting happens in theaters, not in partnership meetings.

Consider the basic math of this timeline. Holmes raised $700 million before criminal indictment. Altman built OpenAI into a $100+ billion valuation in an environment where board members resigned over governance concerns. Zuckerberg converted Facebook into a surveillance monopoly that generated hundreds of billions in market value while regulators scratched their heads. Musk's companies have absorbed billions in venture, government subsidies, and public market capital despite a track record of missed timelines, regulatory violations, and personal conduct that would disqualify most CEOs. The venture community didn't miss these red flags. They bet on them.

What's particularly acidic about four major films dropping simultaneously is that they create a false sense of reckoning. Audiences will watch these narratives and feel like justice is being served, like the system is finally holding power accountable. Meanwhile, venture firms are already funding the next generation of charismatic founders with identical playbooks: the absolute conviction that rules don't apply, the willingness to exaggerate or fabricate, the gravitational pull that makes capital orbit incompetence. The films are an exorcism—a way for Hollywood to pretend it's morally vigilant while the actual power structures that enabled these figures remain unchanged.

The real horror show isn't on screen. It's the realization that venture capital will fund the next Musk, Zuckerberg, Altman, or Holmes without hesitation, because the incentive structure hasn't shifted. Returns reward speed and scale, not ethics or accuracy. By the time the third act resolves and the credits roll, another unicorn will be raising Series B on the back of founder mythology that investors know, deep down, is curated fiction. Hollywood gets to play moral arbiter. Venture gets to play ignorant and rich. The cycle continues.

At least the popcorn will be good.
glossary_definition: VC-speak for describing a founder's personal neuroses and ethical blindspots as competitive advantages that justify unlimited capital allocation and governance exemptions.
